title: Articles
summary: Choose de, het or een, and learn nouns together with their article.

sections.title: De and het
sections.text: Both mean “the”. Use de with common-gender nouns and all definite plurals. Use het with neuter singular nouns and singular diminutives. Learn the article as part of each noun; a word merely ending in the letters je is not automatically a diminutive.

sections.title: Een and no article
sections.text: Een means “a/an” and is normally unstressed. It works with singular countable de- and het-words. There is no indefinite plural article. General uncountable nouns often appear without an article; specific ones can take an article.

examples.en: The books are on the table.

tips: Learn het huis, not just huis.
A singular diminutive takes het; its plural takes de: het huisje → de huisjes.

quiz.explanation: All definite plural nouns take de.
Huisje is a singular diminutive, so it takes het.

title: Personal pronouns
summary: Choose the subject: who is doing the action?

sections.title: Subject forms
sections.text: Subject pronouns replace the person or thing doing the action. Zij/ze can mean “she” or “they”; the verb and context show which one.

sections.title: Emphasis and politeness
sections.text: Jij, wij and zij are useful for emphasis or contrast; je, we and ze are common neutral forms in speech and writing. Use u for polite address, with a singular verb even when addressing several people. Jullie is informal plural. Forms such as ’k and -ie are mainly colloquial.

examples.nl: Ik woon in Nederland, en jij?
examples.en: I live in the Netherlands, and you?

examples.nl: Ze woont hier. / Ze wonen hier.
examples.en: She lives here. / They live here.

tips: Use the full form when contrasting people: jij, not je.
Zij is not always plural: check woont versus wonen.

quiz.explanation: Wij is plural and takes luisteren.
Jullie means informal plural “you”.

title: Possessive pronouns
summary: Say whose something is, and choose ons or onze.

sections.title: Possessives before a noun
sections.text: Use mijn, je/jouw, uw, zijn, haar, ons/onze, jullie or hun before the thing owned. The noun being owned determines ons versus onze, not the owner.

sections.title: Ons or onze
sections.text: Use ons before a singular het-word: ons huis. Use onze before a singular de-word and before all plural nouns: onze docent, onze huizen.

sections.title: Other ways to express ownership
sections.text: Use van + name/object pronoun: het boek van Anna; het boek is van haar. Names normally take a joined -s (Jans boek). After a long vowel written as one letter, use apostrophe + s (Anna’s boek, Felicia’s boek). After an s-sound, use only an apostrophe (Kees’ boek).

examples.en: Our teacher comes from the Netherlands.

tips: Je can mean “you” or “your”: check its role in the sentence.
Uw is possessive; u is a subject or object pronoun.

quiz.explanation: Huis is a singular het-word: ons huis.
All plural nouns take onze.

title: Object pronouns
summary: Use mij, jou, hem, haar, het, ons and ze as objects.

sections.title: Subject versus object
sections.text: Use object forms for the person receiving an action and after a preposition: ik → mij/me, jij → jou/je, hij → hem, zij → haar, wij → ons. Full forms carry emphasis; reduced forms are often neutral.

sections.title: Referring to things
sections.text: For many singular de-words, Dutch uses hij/hem: de trui → ik koop hem. Het-words use het: het boek → ik lees het. Some feminine nouns take zij/haar; natural gender and usage matter. Plural things use ze.

sections.title: Hen, hun and ze
sections.text: For people, the traditional written rule uses hen as direct object and after a preposition, and hun as indirect object without a preposition. Unstressed ze is often a natural alternative in both object roles. Do not use hun as a standard subject pronoun.

examples.nl: Waar is het boek? Ik zie het niet.
examples.en: Where is the book? I do not see it.

examples.nl: Ik koop tomaten. Ik koop ze op de markt.
examples.en: I buy tomatoes. I buy them at the market.

tips: Use jou after a preposition: met jou. Jouw means “your”.
For plural things, use ze rather than hen.

quiz.explanation: After met, use an object form: mij.

quiz.prompt: Waar is het boek? Ik lees ___.
quiz.explanation: Het boek is a het-word, so the pronoun is het.

title: Regular verbs
summary: Build the present tense from the stem and use the finite verb in the right place.

sections.title: Build the stem
sections.text: Start from the infinitive without -en and adjust spelling: wonen → woon, maken → maak, werken → werk, leven → leef, reizen → reis. Preserve the vowel sound and standard spelling.

sections.title: Present tense
sections.text: Ik uses the stem. Jij/je, u and hij/zij/het normally use stem + t. If the stem already ends in t, do not add another t. All plural subjects use the infinitive.

sections.title: Inversion
sections.text: When jij/je is the subject after the finite verb, drop the added -t: jij werkt → werk jij? Keep a t belonging to the stem: jij zit → zit jij? U keeps the usual ending: werkt u? In a declarative main clause, the finite verb is in the second constituent position.

examples.en: We live in the Netherlands now.
Do you also live in Utrecht?

tips: Je must be the subject for the inversion rule: Werkt je vader? keeps -t because vader is the subject.
A second position is a sentence part, not necessarily the second word.

quiz.explanation: The subject je follows the verb, so the added -t disappears.
U keeps stem + t, including in questions.

title: Hebben & zijn
summary: Learn the irregular present forms of “to have” and “to be”.

sections.title: Irregular singular forms
sections.text: Memorise heb/hebt/heeft and ben/bent/is. Plurals are hebben and zijn. The polite u can take hebt or heeft; with zijn, use bent.

sections.title: Questions and inversion
sections.text: Jij hebt → heb jij? Jij bent → ben jij? The ending -t disappears with subject jij/je after the verb. It stays with u: hebt u? bent u?

examples.en: When do you have a break?

tips: Iedereen is grammatically singular: iedereen heeft.
Learn these forms first: they also build the perfect tense.

quiz.explanation: With jij after the verb, bent becomes ben.
Iedereen takes the third-person singular form heeft.

title: Inversion
summary: Start with time or another element while keeping the finite verb second.

sections.title: The V2 rule
sections.text: In a declarative main clause the finite verb occupies position two. Position one can be the subject, a time expression, an object or another constituent. A whole phrase such as om elf uur counts as one constituent.

sections.title: Move the subject after the verb
sections.text: When another constituent takes the first position, the subject follows the finite verb: Ik werk morgen → Morgen werk ik. This is inversion.

sections.title: Questions have their own pattern
sections.text: A yes/no question starts with the finite verb: Werk je morgen? A question word can come first: Waar woon je? These are not exceptions to a rule for declarative main clauses; they are different sentence patterns.

tips: Keep a whole phrase together: Om elf uur | hebben | we | pauze.
Drop the added -t when subject jij/je follows the verb.

quiz.explanation: Morgen is first, werk second, then the subject ik.
The full time phrase counts as one constituent.

title: Time, manner & place
summary: A useful neutral order for the middle of a Dutch sentence.

sections.title: A practical starting pattern
sections.text: After subject + finite verb, a common neutral sequence is time → manner/means/company → place/destination. Ask wanneer? hoe/met wie? waar/waarnaartoe?

sections.title: Use it as a guide, not an absolute law
sections.text: Dutch word order can change with emphasis, information structure and the type of phrase. A time phrase at the end is not automatically ungrammatical. These examples teach a reliable beginner pattern, not every possible order.

sections.title: Combine it with the verb bracket
sections.text: With a modal or the perfect tense, the infinitive or participle normally comes after the middle: Ik wil morgen met de trein naar Utrecht gaan. If time is first, use inversion: Morgen ga ik met de trein naar Utrecht.

examples.nl: Ik ga morgen met mijn vrienden naar het park.
examples.en: I am going to the park with my friends tomorrow.

examples.nl: Morgen ga ik met de trein naar Utrecht.
examples.en: Tomorrow I am going to Utrecht by train.

examples.nl: Ik fiets in de ochtend snel naar de supermarkt.
examples.en: I cycle quickly to the supermarket in the morning.

tips: First build a short correct sentence, then add when, how and where.
Time–manner–place is a neutral default, not a test that makes every other order wrong.

quiz.explanation: Met de trein tells us the means of transport.

options: Ik ga morgen met de trein naar Utrecht.
Ik morgen ga met de trein naar Utrecht.
Ik morgen met de trein ga naar Utrecht.
quiz.explanation: The finite verb ga is second; time, means and destination follow.

title: Modal verbs
summary: Express ability, permission, obligation, wishes and suggestions.

sections.title: Meaning
sections.text: Kunnen expresses ability or possibility; mogen permission; moeten necessity; willen a wish; zullen an offer, intention, promise or suggestion. Meaning depends on context.

sections.title: Verb bracket
sections.text: Conjugate the modal in the normal finite-verb position and put the action verb in the infinitive at the end: Ik moet morgen werken. Do not add te after these modals.

sections.title: When the action is understood
sections.text: Dutch can omit an obvious infinitive: Ik wil koffie (hebben/drinken). Ik moet naar de les (gaan). With hij/zij/het, modal forms do not gain a regular extra -t: hij wil, hij kan, hij mag, hij zal.

examples.en: We have to do exercise three.

tips: Hij wil is correct; hij wilt is not standard.
An infinitive stays intact after a modal: ik kan werken.

quiz.explanation: Third-person singular is hij wil, without an added -t.
The action verb after a modal is an infinitive at the end.

title: The perfect tense
summary: Use hebben or zijn plus a past participle to talk about completed events.

sections.title: Build a sentence
sections.text: Use a present form of hebben or zijn as the finite verb, plus a past participle at the end of a simple main clause: Ik heb gisteren gewerkt. English may translate this as “I worked” or “I have worked”, depending on context.

sections.title: Regular participles
sections.text: Usually form ge- + correctly spelled stem + t/d. Use -t for voiceless final stem sounds represented by ’t kofschip (t, k, f, s, ch, p; also relevant loanword sounds such as sj). Otherwise use -d. Check the consonant before -en in the infinitive for v/z: leven → geleefd; reizen → gereisd. Do not decide from leef/reis alone.

sections.title: Prefixes and irregular forms
sections.text: Unstressed inseparable prefixes such as be-, ge-, her-, ont- and ver- normally receive no extra ge-: betaald, gebruikt, herhaald, ontmoet, verhuurd. Memorise irregular participles such as gedronken, geweest, gebleven and geworden. Separable verbs insert ge after the separable prefix: opgebeld.

sections.title: Hebben or zijn
sections.text: Most activities take hebben. Many changes of state and certain verbs take zijn, for example worden, blijven and gebeuren. Movement can use hebben for an activity (ik heb gefietst) and zijn for movement to a destination (ik ben naar huis gefietst). Learn the auxiliary with the verb and construction; movement alone does not guarantee zijn.

examples.nl: We zijn om negen uur begonnen.

tips: Do not add ge- twice: betalen → betaald, not gebetaald.
Learn verb + auxiliary + participle as one unit: blijven → is gebleven.

quiz.explanation: Werk ends in k, so the regular participle is gewerkt.
Movement to a destination takes zijn here; with ik use ben.

title: Separable verbs
summary: Learn what happens to prefixes in statements, modals and the perfect tense.

sections.title: Two parts, one meaning
sections.text: A separable prefix and verb create a new meaning: instappen (board), uitstappen (get off), meenemen (take along), opbellen (phone). Not every prefixed verb is separable; learn the complete verb.

sections.title: Finite main-clause verb
sections.text: In present or simple past main clauses, conjugate the base verb and place the prefix near the end: Ik bel je morgen op. Hij nam de kaart mee. An imperative also separates: Neem de kaart mee! A subordinate clause keeps the finite verb together: omdat ik je opbel.

sections.title: Modal, participle and te
sections.text: After a modal, keep the full infinitive together: Ik wil je opbellen. In the participle, insert ge after the prefix when the base verb takes ge: opgebeld, ingestapt, meegenomen. With te, separate into prefix + te + verb: op te bellen; mee te nemen. Some base verbs, such as betalen, do not take ge: terugbetalen → terugbetaald.

rows: Ik hoef je niet op te bellen.

examples.nl: Hij is bij het station ingestapt.
U hoeft de straat niet over te steken.
examples.en: You do not need to cross the street.

examples.nl: Neemt u de plattegrond maar mee.
examples.en: Please take the map with you.

tips: Meenemen has an irregular base participle: meegenomen, not meegeneemd.
Compare: Ik bel op / ik wil opbellen / ik heb opgebeld / om op te bellen.

quiz.explanation: After a modal, use the full infinitive together.
With te, use prefix + te + base verb.
